newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- US yield curve seen flatter by end'98.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- US yield curve seen flatter by end'98.

text.p: - Sticking to their forecast for a U.S. economic slowdown that proved wrong over the past five quarters, market experts predicted growth will cool off within 12 months, resulting in lower market rates and a flatter Treasury yield curve.

The consensus forecast in a Reuters poll of 29 economists showed the benchmark 5.50-percent federal funds rate rising to 6.00 percent by the third quarter -- only for the Federal Reserve to shave the inter-bank overnight lending by 25 basis points six months later.

Based on the projected back-and-forth moves by the Fed, forecasters expected the three-month Treasury bill yield to average 5.40 percent in the current quarter, climb to 5.75 percent by late 1997 -- and retreat to its present level by late 1998.

Despite the consensus forecast for a higher funds rate this year, market experts felt the 30-year Treasury bond yield has already hit its peak for the current tightening cycle with a recent high at 7.19 percent.
They expected the bond yield to start drifting lower in the third quarter and fall to 6.63 percent by late 1998.
The anticipated long-end rally would narrow the spread between the three-month bill and 30-year bond yields from 179 points in the second quarter to 123 points by late 1998.

In line with expectations of low inflationary pressures, small Fed moves and a slower economy, the 10-year to 30-year yield spread would almost vanish from a current 29 points to 12 points by late 1998, the experts also said.

"It's a safe forecast of not very much change and not very much variables," said Ian Shepherdson, chief economist at HSBC Markets. "I don't disagree with it. But, like all safe forecasts, I would not rule out a surprise."
Shepherdson saw the main challenge to the consensus forecast coming from overseas economies.

"Interest rates might be cut at the end of 1997 or in early 1998 and then go up again because there will likely be a pretty robust recovery in Europe and Japan," said Shepherdson who added this may push the long bond yield to "7.25 percent, which, if it reaches that level, would be pretty good value."

Shepherdson expected U.S growth to slow down from its unsustainable pace of the past two quarters and investment spending to cool off along with corporate profits margins -- factors which would result in a flatter yield curve.

"The biggest risk is that the second-half slowdown will not be quite as marked as expected, the biggest risk is the recovery in Europe and the Far East and that will mean the U.S. economy might not slow down very much," said Shepherdson who saw "one more Fed hike in May, and after that, I am an agnostic."
Dana Johnson, managing director at First Chicago Capital Markets, commenting on the consensus forecast, expected that "things are going to get a little more interesting than that."
Like Shepherdson, Johnson viewed economic growth overseas as the main question mark for the U.S. rate outlook.

"It will depend an awful lot on the rest of the world. If Europe, and Japan do better as I think they will, we are not going to get a reversal of U.S. rates. They are going to drift higher through the end of 1998," Johnson stated.
Johnson viewed risks of rising U.S. inflation as higher than generally accepted.

"We are in that late part of the cycle when growth will resume in other parts of the world and demand for credit there will rise. A reversal of interest rates before a recession emerges in the United States is very unlikely," the First Chicago director said.
Johnson said the Treasury market is overly optimistic about the U.S. inflation outlook.

"There normally is a tremendous inertia in the inflation process unless there is a huge price shock. The view that inflation is going to fall or that the Fed is going to be able to undo that bit of tightening is also very unlikely," the First Chicago director said.

"The high resource utilization, in particular in labor markets, do argue that inflation risks are real. At this stage in the business cycle, the Fed needs to keep real interest rates higher than 2.0 percent," Johnson concluded.
